strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 1,200+ tasks across 9 environments with systematic baselines, real robot deployment on 3 platforms, and extensive ablations demonstrating strong empirical results (93.3% success vs 52.5% best LLM baseline)
Well-motivated practical contribution: Addresses real bottleneck in TAMP by automating PDDL domain derivation without manual engineering, reducing deployment barriers for robotics applications
Complete system automation: LoCA automatically interfaces symbolic actions with motion planners, eliminating labor-intensive manual alignment and improving usability

Clear presentation and reproducibility support: Well-written with comprehensive supplementary material including detailed prompts, prompt templates, experimental protocols, and multiple variants enabling understanding
Robust methodology: Two-stage predicate generation (first-order then higher-order) and parallel prompting strategy are principled approaches; demonstrated stability across prompt variations
Superior efficiency: Significantly lower token costs than reasoning LLMs while achieving better performance; faster time-to-solution than LLM-based baselines
weaknesses: Limited component novelty: Predicate imagination follows prior work (Curtis et al. 2022, Silver et al. 2023); action invention from state transitions is straightforward; main contribution is combining existing techniques with single demonstrations, which is primarily engineering-focused and incremental

Misleading 'single demonstration' framing: Compositional tasks require multiple demonstrations (rearrangement: stack+unstack; bridge building: stack+align); complex domains show 22.2% missing predicates; more accurate to acknowledge multiple demonstration requirement

Significant scope limitations: Restricted to tabletop manipulation with discrete rigid objects; no evaluation on continuous state spaces, deformable objects, temporal constraints, or complex geometric reasoning; severely limits applicability beyond narrow problem class

Scalability concerns and performance degradation: Strong performance degradation on complex domains (bridge building 87.2% vs 100% expert; burger cooking 91.7%; rearrangement 64.3% vs 73.3%); 22.2% missing predicates indicates fundamental challenges; requires 'thousands of parallel simulations' without cost analysis

Problematic expert baseline: 'Expert design' initialized from PDDLLM outputs then refined by human—not independent comparison; does not represent truly expert-designed domains from scratch; undermines claims about domain quality relative to expert design

Limited real robot validation: Only brief demonstrations; domains unevenly tested across platforms (bridge building only Franka, burger cooking only Agilex); no systematic evaluation of sim-to-real transfer or robustness to real-world variations; physical constraints effectiveness in practice unclear

Heavy LLM dependency: Exclusively uses GPT-4o; no analysis of failure modes; RuleAsMem ablation (69.9% success) shows LLMs struggle even with perfect symbolic domains but this is insufficiently discussed; unclear how method generalizes to weaker LLMs

Missing comparative evaluations: No comparison with recent domain learning approaches (VisualPredicator cited but not compared); limited comparison with other LLM-based domain generation methods; reasoning models evaluated with different time budgets (500s vs 50s)

Incomplete analysis: Arbitrary design choices lack justification (why 5 parallel prompts?); limited failure mode analysis; unclear when practitioners should use this vs. manual design; no computational cost breakdown; weak discussion of when/why approach fails on complex domains

Reproducibility and generalizability concerns: Relies on expensive GPT-4o API calls; requires specific simulation setup; no code/data release mentioned; difficult to reproduce or extend; unclear how approach scales to more complex domains

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem (automating PDDL domain design)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 1,200 tasks with multiple baselines and ablations
Strong empirical results relative to LLM-based planning baselines (93.3% vs 52.5%)
Successfully demonstrated on real robots across three different platforms
Extensive supplementary materials with detailed ablations and documentation
Achieves performance comparable to expert-designed domains in many task categories
weaknesses: Central claims are overclaimed: 'One Demo' claim is misleading (requires multiple demos for complex tasks; bridge building needs both stacking and alignment demos); 'no manual predesign' claim contradicted by requirement to manually define feature spaces and subspace intervals (critical hyperparameters)

Limited technical novelty: core components are straightforward applications of existing ideas (LLM summarization of simulation rollouts, state transition recognition from demonstrations, constraint extraction for motion planning)

Unfair baseline comparisons: PDDLLM receives demonstration trajectories plus simulator access plus feature space specification, while LLMTAMP receives only natural language descriptions—these are inequivalent inputs
Fundamental unresolved limitation: Table 3 shows 22.2% missing predicates in complex domains with no principled solution (Burger Cooking/Bridge Building drop to 91.7%/87.2% vs 100% for expert)
Brittleness to incomplete demonstrations: Table 4 shows performance drops to 0% with missing skills, tested on only one task with no systematic procedure for identifying missing actions
Limited scope: nine 'environments' are primarily manipulation task variants, not diverse domains; all evaluated in PyBullet simulation; no navigation, continuous control, or abstract reasoning tasks

Heavy reliance on prompt engineering despite claims otherwise: Section A.3 shows detailed prompts; parallel prompting (5+ candidates) hedges against brittleness; Section A.7 shows robustness only to minor variations
LLM-dependent: all domain derivation uses GPT-4o; unclear how method generalizes to other LLMs; cost implications not discussed
LoCA contribution is overstated: extracting constraints from predicates and passing to motion planner is straightforward constraint grounding, extensively studied in TAMP literature
Hyperparameter sensitivity: feature subspace size is critical but no systematic exploration; minimal guidance for practitioners on setting parameters for new domains

strengths: Clear and timely contribution: automates PDDL domain generation from demonstrations, addressing significant bottleneck in TAMP systems
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: 1,200 tasks across 9 environments, multiple well-chosen baselines, real robot deployment on 3 platforms
Strong empirical results: 93.3% success rate vs 35.7-52.5% for LLM baselines, comparable to expert-designed domains (95.7%)
Well-designed system architecture combining physical simulation for feasibility with LLM reasoning for semantics; LoCA provides practical automatic motion planning integration
Excellent reproducibility: extensive implementation details, prompt templates, complete experimental documentation in appendix
Good experimental methodology: proper ablations, robustness testing (prompt variations, suboptimal demonstrations), generalization analysis across task complexity
Demonstrates knowledge compositionality with modular PDDL actions transferring across related tasks
Clear presentation with effective illustrations and examples; good balance between main paper and appendix
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (simulation-based feasibility + LLM summarization, logical state grounding) are straightforward applications of existing techniques; main contribution is systems integration rather than methodological innovation

Acknowledged scalability limitations with domain complexity: success rates drop to 64-87% in harder tasks (Rearrangement, Bridge Building), with 22% missing predicates in most complex domains; limited analysis of why predicates are missed or systematic solutions
Scope limitations: all tasks are discrete object manipulation in structured environments; unclear generalization to continuous control, deformable objects, or complex geometric constraints
Expert baseline fairness: expert-designed domains are refined from PDDLLM-derived domains rather than independently created, making the performance gap interpretation difficult
Misleading framing: 'one demo' for compositional tasks actually uses separate demonstrations per skill (stack, unstack, align); could be clearer in title/abstract
Incomplete analysis of missing predicates: no systematic breakdown by type, limited investigation of whether additional demonstrations improve coverage, insufficient exploration of failure modes

Hyperparameter sensitivity under-explored: feature space discretization interval length and parallel prompting threshold (5) appear empirically chosen without sensitivity analysis or principled justification
Limited theoretical analysis: no formal framework for predicting when/why the approach succeeds or fails; complexity analysis (A.10.2) is descriptive rather than prescriptive

Motion planning integration details limited: unclear how robust LoCA is when physical constraints are imprecise; real robot experiments show success but lack constraint vs. alternative approaches comparison
Comparison methodology: extended time limits for reasoning models (500s vs 50s) make fairness of practical deployment comparison less direct

strengths: Addresses a genuine bottleneck in TAMP—manual domain construction is labor-intensive and limits scalability
Thoughtful technical design combining LLM reasoning with physical simulation verification to ground outputs in physics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 1,200 tasks across 9 environments with extensive ablations and real robot validation on 3 platforms
Strong empirical results: 93.3% success (40% improvement over best LLM baseline, comparable to expert-designed domains at 95.7%)
LoCA contribution for automatic motion planner integration eliminates manual constraint engineering
Demonstrates compositional action reuse and knowledge transfer across tasks
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendix with prompts, hyperparameters, and implementation details
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2) communicating the overall approach
weaknesses: Misleading title and 'one demo' claim: compositional tasks require multiple subtask demonstrations (Table 4 shows 0% success with partial demos), contradicting headline claims
Fundamental limitation inadequately addressed: system frequently misses complex predicates (22.2% missing rate, Table 3) requiring manual refinement, undermining 'minimal manual effort' claims
Significant simulation-to-reality gap: real robot success 70-90% vs simulation 93.3%; predicate accuracy drops to 74% with 30% perception noise; entire approach depends on reliable simulators

Limited domain scope despite generality claims: restricted to classical TAMP with consistent object properties and PyBullet simulators; doesn't handle deformable objects, fluids, contact-rich manipulation
Overclaimed automation: requires manual hyperparameter tuning (u discretization, parallel prompt count 5-15), feature space bounds definition, and missing predicate additions
Unfair expert baseline comparison: expert designs refined from PDDLLM outputs (not from scratch), making small performance gap (95.7% vs 93.3%) misleading about manual effort

Limited technical novelty: predicate imagination (sampling + LLM), action invention (state transition extraction), and LoCA (constraint mapping) are individually relatively straightforward; contribution is primarily system integration
Ad-hoc design choices: parallel prompting with majority voting lacks principled justification; convergence at 5 prompts not explained; 8.3% domain generation failure rate even at this threshold

Incomplete scalability analysis: complexity formula shows n^(n_dim) exponential factor; claim of 'linear growth' not well-supported; high-dimensional feature handling via decomposition is pragmatic but ad-hoc

Knowledge transfer claims overstated: tested only on simple compositional scenarios (combining stack+alignment); no evidence of handling truly novel task compositions with unexpected predicate interactions

strengths: Tackles a practically important problem of automating PDDL domain construction from demonstrations, addressing real challenges in robotics planning
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 1,200+ tasks spanning 9 different environments with multiple baselines and extensive ablation studies
Real-world validation on three different robot platforms (Franka Panda, Agilex Piper, UR5e) demonstrates practical applicability beyond simulation
Extensive implementation details, hyperparameter studies, and ablations provided in appendix supporting reproducibility
Useful practical contribution via LoCA component that automatically interfaces symbolic plans with motion planning constraints
Demonstrates flexibility by showing compatibility with both classical motion planning and learning-based control (VLA) approaches
weaknesses: Core claims significantly overstated - 'one demo is all it takes' is misleading given requirements for manual feature space specification, discretization scale selection (u_f), 10-20 parallel prompts, thousands of simulation rollouts, and manual task descriptions
Contradicts 'one demo' claim by using multiple demonstrations of subtasks for compositional tasks (rearrangement, bridge building), not single demonstrations as title suggests

Limited technical novelty - primary contributions are incremental: discretizing feature space and prompting LLM to summarize simulated interactions (straightforward), mechanically applying logical operators for higher-order predicates (rigid template-based), parallel prompting with majority voting (crude engineering workaround), and constraint extraction via LoCA (mechanical, not novel)
Unfair experimental methodology - expert baseline is refined from PDDLLM outputs rather than independently designed, making comparison fundamentally biased in favor of PDDLLM
Scope limited to simple manipulation tasks well-suited to TAMP framework with no evidence of generalization to domains outside this narrow setting or tasks requiring many features/predicates
Significant performance degradation on complex tasks (Bridge Building: 87.2±4.3%, Burger Cooking: 91.7±4.8%) and real robots (70-80% success), contradicting scalability claims
Method cannot recover from missing predicates - Table 3 shows 22.2% missing predicates in complex domains (bridge building, burger cooking) with no automatic recovery mechanism
Perception robustness insufficient - accuracy drops to ~80% with only 20% injected noise; real robot experiments show further performance loss despite perfect simulation conditions
Critical missing analysis: no demonstration of actual time/effort savings compared to manually writing PDDL domains - the fundamental efficiency claim is never validated
Unaddressed sim-to-real gap - real robot success rates (70-90%) are substantially lower than simulation (87-100%) but limited investigation of causes or mitigation
Arbitrary experimental choices bias results - 50-second time limit heavily favors pre-computed domains over reasoning LLMs; comparison at 500 seconds feels post-hoc
Feature space specification treated as solved when it requires significant domain knowledge; no principled guidance on choosing features or handling insufficient feature spaces for new domains

Scalability analysis incomplete - assumes linear growth in predicate types but real domains often require exponential combinations of features; domain derivation complexity bounds up to 128 are concerning

Incomplete methodological analysis of demonstration quality sensitivity - Table 4 only tests bridge building with missing demonstrations; no systematic study of noisy, suboptimal, or misleading demonstrations
Overstated novelty claims - 'first approach to generate complete planning domain from scratch' is debatable when substantial initialization and domain knowledge specification is required

strengths: Addresses a real bottleneck in TAMP: automating labor-intensive PDDL domain engineering
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 1,200+ tasks across 9 environments with systematic complexity analysis and multiple strong baselines
Strong empirical results: 93.3% success rate vs. 52.5% for best LLM baseline, comparable to expert-designed domains (95.7%)
Real robot validation on three platforms (Franka Panda, Agilex Piper, UR5e) demonstrates practical applicability
Well-motivated technical approach combining simulation for feasibility verification with LLM reasoning for abstraction
Extensive ablation studies examining hyperparameters, prompting strategies, and LLM backbones
Practical system design with automatic motion planner integration (LoCA) and VLA compatibility
Exceptional reproducibility: 42-page appendix with implementation details, prompts, and supplementary studies
Demonstrates effective knowledge transfer across tasks (compositional learning for rearrangement and bridge building)
Efficient token usage compared to reasoning models (415K vs. 1200K+ for o1-TAMP)
weaknesses: Title oversells contribution: 'One demo is all it takes' is misleading—complex tasks require demonstrations of multiple simpler subtasks, and requires 10 parallel prompts with hyperparameter tuning
Limited technical novelty: combines well-established techniques (simulation, LLM prompting, PDDL); individual components are not novel
Significant sim-to-real gap: simulation achieves 93.3% success but real-world performance is 70-90% (Table 5); limited analysis of failure modes in deployment
Reliance on perfect simulators: approach fundamentally limited to domains with good physics simulators; scalability to domains requiring accurate simulation of complex dynamics unclear

Missing complex predicates problem: 0-22.2% missing predicates even on known tasks (Table 3); complex predicates like (all_base_finished) are hard to learn but critical for planning efficiency (Section B.17)
Circular expert baseline: Expert Design initialized from PDDLLM outputs rather than independent from scratch, making gap assessment unreliable
Scope limitations: evaluation restricted to tabletop manipulation with simple features (position, size, color); no temporal constraints, complex interactions, or high-dimensional states
Hyperparameter sensitivity: Critical parameters (u_f, n_prompts) require tuning; 41.7% failure rate with single prompt vs. 8.3% with 10 prompts (Section B.16); limited guidance for new domains
Domain derivation cost: 300-550K tokens per domain (Table 18) is expensive; no discussion of amortization for multiple related tasks
Scalability not validated: largest tested domain is 128 predicates; no empirical evidence for claimed linear scaling to complex domains with 1000+ predicates
Demonstration quality: assumes near-optimal demonstrations; limited systematic study of degradation with suboptimal or noisy human demonstrations beyond Table 4
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: when does the method fail? What predicates are fundamentally hard to learn? How does complexity affect success probability?
Homogeneous evaluation environments: nine environments all similar (tabletop manipulation); no diversity in domain types (navigation, deformables, temporal constraints, etc.)
